How do I become a computer/internet wizard like the rest of you?

Honestly a lot of it comes through tinkering. You can learn anything you want about computers by googling it, but the best way is to actually work with whatever it is you want to do. Want to learn about Linux? Make a Linux boot device and mess around with it! Want to learn about VPNs? Check out Hotspot Shield or something. Programming? Try w3Schools.

As far as languages go, if you want to learn one, I would recommend C# or Java. They are widely used and relatively easy to pick up with little to no experience.

For Linux distros I would recommend Ubuntu or Linux Mint as a good starting distro. It has plenty of tools preinstalled for beginners (especially Ubuntu).
In this context a distro (or distribution) is a particular version of a linux OS.
So it's like the model of a car and Linux is the make?

It makes a lot more sense when you learn - or remind yourself - that "Linux" itself is actually a really small part of the system, the "kernel" that actually runs computation, memory management, and other extremely basic parts of running a computer system.

If you only had the kernel on a system, it'd be essentially useless. The kernel does not include the programs to boot the system up, to draw a user interface on the screen, or to do any of the things that you want a computer for.

So the Linux kernel isn't really used on its own, because it's not much use to... users. Instead, it's packaged up with a bunch of other programs that do all those other things so that a computer is actually a useful tool. So linux is "distributed" - I mean, actually burned onto a disc or downloaded from a server, that kind of distribution - as a really big collection of programs that happen to have Linux running as the kernel.

That's why they're called "distributions." I hope that makes sense. It's kind of hard to explain to people who aren't already used to it.

For a Linux beginner, the important thing is that everything you touch is part of the distribution but not part of the linux kernel itself. So different distributions will look different depending on what software was included, and it's important to shop around a bit to find one that works for you.
That makes a lot of sense. Thanks for a good explanation

You're welcome! I'm glad the point got across because I'm generally pretty shit at teaching people things. XD

As long as I'm here, though, I'd like to add that the Linux kernel isn't the only thing that a lot of distributions share, which my last comment might have implied. For example, most Linux distributions with a "Windows-like" desktop use one of two systems to draw that desktop: GTK or Qt. Many of them can run one or the other or both at the same time depending on how you set them up.

If you're interested in getting your hands dirty with this stuff, I'll strongly recommend looking at Ubuntu or Mint. Both are based on Debian, which is an extremely versatile and popular distribution, but not quite as user-friendly. Once you get comfortable with your first distro - you've broken things and managed to fix them a few times - you'll be able to apply most of the same skills to running Debian.

The point is, every distribution is different, but they're similar enough that you shouldn't be too worried about switching between them. Pick one you like, learn it, then go explore a bit. Patience and a willingness to experiment are greatly rewarded in the Linux world.

I would say that there are four distinct parts of "computer wizardry" that people specialize into.

First, Hardware. Usually, these guys like upgrading their computers for the most badass of specs, most often for gaming than anything else. Probably the most fun (when you consider the finished product), but also the most expensive.

Second, Operating Systems. Usually revolved around setting up schedules and perfecting your operating system so that it's more "you", this is for people who like to be in control on a budget. Programming and Networking kinda fit in here, and most people that are decent in this section prefer Linux as an operating system.

Third, Programming. This is for your creators and inventors. Building something from the ground up with just your intellect. Uses a lot of math and understanding how systems work. Python is a solid starting language, Java and C are also very common. If you want to start with something really easy and fun, give Game Maker a shot.

Fourth, Networking. VPNs fall into here, so does many different types of protection. Learning new (and some common sense) ways of protecting yourself or a business is actually quite fun, IMO. A good program to teach yourself how to network is Packet Tracer, which simulates a network building environment on your computer, so you don't have to actually have 100 different computers to test in real life.
